claims.text: The material family of interest is multiphase Al-containing refractory high-entropy alloys with BCC and B2 phases.
The primary mechanical property of interest is room-temperature ductility or fracture strain after aging.
The solutionized initial state contains a disordered BCC matrix with weak or incipient B2 ordering.
The solutionized initial state contains fine coherent precipitates.
Aging at 600–900 °C promotes B2 precipitate growth and ordering and may form Heusler or Laves phases.
The aging temperature must be high enough for ordering diffusion but below the B2 solvus.
A largely single-phase disordered BCC matrix in solutionized Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr permits substantial strain hardening and high ductility.
A high volume fraction of needle-like Heusler phase degrades ductility and produces brittle fracture.
Excessive chemical ordering causes the proposed intermediate ductile-to-brittle transition.
A reticulated Laves-phase network can hinder crack propagation and offset ductility loss from a brittle phase.
Prolonged aging can transform the brittle secondary phase into a reticulated morphology that restores ductility.
Precipitate coarsening reduces interfacial stress concentrations and permits dislocation transfer across coherent interfaces.
The alloys will exhibit a ductile-brittle-ductile dependence of elongation on aging time.
Long-time ductility recovery may occur through restoration of interface coherency.
A brittle-phase volume fraction below approximately 10% is required to avoid catastrophic failure.
Whether a brittle secondary phase is reticulated or granular affects its influence on crack propagation and ductility.
The role of the Heusler phase in mechanical behavior is not fully clarified in the cited literature.
The transition time window depends strongly on ordering and phase-separation kinetics and therefore on composition, including Al content.
A time-series aging experiment at 700 °C with room-temperature tensile testing can falsify the hypothesis if ductility remains monotonic or fails to recover after a reticulated phase forms.

contradictions.description: The mediator proposes progression from coherent to semi-coherent or incoherent interfaces, while the recovery mechanism invokes dislocation transfer across coherent interfaces and the outcome invokes restoration of coherency. No process that would reverse the coherency loss is specified.

A continuous network of brittle phases is first presented as the cause of embrittlement, but a reticulated continuous network is later presented as the cause of ductility recovery. The distinction between harmful and beneficial continuous networks is not defined clearly enough by phase identity, fraction, or topology.
